summary.text: A 24-year-old nulliparous primigravida with pregestational, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes had been hospitalized one year before pregnancy for severe hyperglycemia with ketonuria, was switched to oral therapy and self-discontinued follow-up. She was referred at 9 weeks of gestation and started basal-bolus insulin with requirements rising to detemir 54 units at bedtime and aspart 38 units before each meal by late pregnancy.

At 35 weeks of gestation she presented with worsening nausea; fetal monitoring showed tachycardia, reduced variability and recurrent variable decelerations consistent with non-reassuring fetal status, and she was admitted as an emergency. On admission she had Kussmaul respiration and DKA was confirmed (glucose 455 mg/dL, pH 7.24, bicarbonate 10.9 mmol/L, 2 + ketonuria). Emergency cesarean delivery was planned and performed before complete stabilization.

Endocrinologists started insulin infusion, an insulin aspart bolus, glucose infusion and saline resuscitation. In the operating room she received an arterial line and combined spinal-epidural anesthesia (bupivacaine, fentanyl, morphine) with phenylephrine, a crystalloid bolus and left uterine displacement; systolic pressure fell to 68 mmHg and was corrected with ephedrine. Surgery followed a bilateral T4 sensory block, insulin was reduced to 1 U/h, skin-closure gas showed pH 7.29, and the epidural catheter was removed immediately postoperatively.

Table 1 lists serial arterial blood gas and laboratory values from hospital admission to 12 h postoperative; pH rose from 7.24 to 7.36 and bicarbonate from 10.9 to 17.1 mmol/L, with some admission values not available in the medical records. She went to the ICU with insulin, glucose, potassium, fluids, analgesia, enoxaparin and ABG monitoring, moved to subcutaneous insulin and oral intake on POD 2, and was discharged on POD 7 without complications.

The authors describe possible DKA precipitants (late-gestation insulin resistance, persistent hyperglycemia, reduced intake due to nausea, possible suboptimal adherence), and note obesity and a short fasting interval.
The 2,456 g female neonate had Apgar scores of 9/10 and an umbilical artery pH of 7.17, and was admitted to the NICU.

The neonate's initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.16, bicarbonate 18.2 mmol/L, lactate 5.6 mmol/L and glucose 131 mg/dL consistent with metabolic acidosis; 2 h later it had spontaneously resolved (pH 7.23, bicarbonate 25.4, lactate 2.2, glucose 114). The neonate remained stable and was discharged on day 18 without complications.

article_limitations: Single index patient (the mother, "A 24-year-old nulliparous woman"); the neonate and the fetal tracing are recorded inside p1 with subject newborn or fetus and are not separate patients, so the roster is one patient and complete.
Fetal monitoring findings are annotated under p1 with subject fetus; they are not copied to the newborn.
Table 1 dashes are recorded as not reported in the medical records, not as zero or normal; the three affected cells are PaO2, base excess and lactate at hospital admission.
Text pH 7.34 by POD 1 cites Table 1 but matches no Table 1 cell; it is review_only. Glucose 261 mg/dL by POD 1 equals the 6 h postoperative cell but is kept separate without reconciliation.

Figure 2 prints values (ephedrine 4 mg, oxytocin 5U doses, blood loss, amniotic fluid, urine output, anesthesia and surgical times) that the text does not state; these live in the visual submission and are not annotated as text facts.
Author-suggested DKA precipitants are interpretation and are recorded as possible, review-only.
Caption-layer visual status not_inspected; the two JPEGs were inspected in the separate visual submission.

Order of operating-room arrival, spinal anesthesia, delivery and placental delivery rests on the Figure 2 caption, which states that these events are annotated along the x-axis timeline, and on the figure axis itself.
